sections.title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

questions.q: Which ability separates humans from animals?
questions.answer: Language.

questions.q: What is the purpose of language in society?
questions.answer: To communicate ideas, share feelings, understand each other and build social relationships.

questions.q: Why is language crucial for young children?
questions.answer: It is a key for thinking, learning and making sense of the world, and it supports cognition; its development goes with brain growth.

questions.q: Why are the early years considered critical for language development?
questions.answer: Language develops very rapidly then, and any stimulation given at this age has a significant impact.

questions.q: During which period does language develop at a very rapid pace?
questions.answer: From birth up to the age of six years.

questions.q: What are the four skills of language learning?
questions.answer: Listening, speaking, reading and writing.

sections.passage: Language is the ability that separates humans from animals. As humans in society, we use our language ability continuously to communicate our ideas, share our feelings, understand each other and build social relationships. Language is an essential key for thinking, learning and making sense of the world around. Language also equips us to revisit events in the past and plan for the future. Most importantly, language serves as a tool to support cognition and vice-versa. Language development goes hand in hand with growth and maturation of the brain. The early years of life are considered critical periods for language development. From birth up to the age of six years, children develop language at a very rapid pace. Any stimulation given at this age for language development significantly impacts children. Language occurs both receptively and expressively through listening, speaking, reading and writing. (April 2026)

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Differentiate between the pre-moral level and the level of conventional morality given by Kohlberg.
questions.answer: At the pre-moral level, children learn right and wrong from people around them; conduct is decided by external factors — approval or disapproval of authority, rewards and punishment — so behaviour is oriented to obedience. At the conventional level, children understand relationships and moral codes and believe rules can be changed if they do not serve the common good of society.

or.q: Describe the heteronomous and autonomous stages of moral development.
or.answer: Piaget's heteronomous stage: children see rules as universal, fixed and handed down by authority; they cannot be changed and anyone who breaks them is punished. Autonomous stage: older children see rules as made for everyone's benefit, so a rule that does not benefit all can be changed by common consensus.

questions.q: What are motor skills? What are the two broad types of motor skills children develop?
questions.answer: Motor skills are physical abilities that help children control the movements of their bodies. The two types are gross motor skills, using large muscles (crawling, walking, running, climbing), and fine motor skills, using small muscles of the hands and fingers with eye-hand coordination (holding a crayon, buttoning, drawing).

questions.q: What are the components of physical growth and development?
questions.answer: Increase in height and weight, changes in body proportions, development of bones (size, proportion, density), maturation of internal organs including the brain and nervous system, and the development of gross and fine motor skills.

questions.q: What is moral development?
questions.answer: Moral development is the growth of a sense of right and wrong ('moral' comes from mores — manners and customs). It includes moral behaviour (acting rightly), moral reasoning (weighing options as right or wrong) and judgment, and proceeds through stages described by Piaget and Kohlberg.

questions.q: What is meant by eye-hand coordination?
questions.answer: The ability to match the movements of the hands with what the eyes see. It is part of fine motor development and helps children hold a cup or crayon, thread beads, draw, cut and write.

questions.q: What are gross motor skills? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Gross motor skills involve the large muscles and control big body movements. Examples: crawling, standing, walking, climbing, running, jumping.
questions.note: April 2023 asked for a one-sentence explanation of gross motor development.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: How does physical-motor development contribute to overall growth and development in children?
questions.answer: Growth of bones, muscles and internal organs including the brain gives the body its strength and form. Gross motor skills let children move, explore and play, which builds cognition and social contact; fine motor skills and eye-hand coordination allow self-help (feeding, dressing) and later drawing and writing. Physical confidence builds self-esteem, and since domains are interrelated, a healthy, active child participates and learns better.

questions.q: What are the two stages of moral development according to Jean Piaget?
questions.answer: Piaget studied children's understanding of rules in play. Heteronomous stage: rules are universal, fixed and given by an outside authority; they cannot be changed and breaking them brings punishment, so children show little flexibility. Autonomous stage: as they grow, children see rules as made for the good of all; a rule that does not benefit everyone can be changed by common consensus.

questions.q: Describe the characteristics of the pre-operational stage of cognitive development.
questions.answer: The pre-operational stage (2–7 years) is pre-logical. Animistic thinking: non-living things that move are thought to be alive. Egocentrism: the child thinks everyone sees things as she does. Lack of reversibility: cannot trace an action back to its start. Lack of conservation: thinks a tall glass has more water than a wide one with the same amount. Children also cannot classify by more than one feature or take multiple perspectives.

questions.q: Describe the development of language in children.
questions.answer: Infants communicate by crying, laughing and cooing; around four months they play with sounds; from 6–7 months cooing becomes babbling ('baba', 'mama'); they also use gestures. These are pre-speech forms. Speech forms follow: comprehension develops before speech, pronunciation becomes clear, vocabulary grows rapidly, and children move from two- or three-word phrases ('give me food') to sentences and complex sentences. In middle childhood they learn the social rules of using language with different people.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Define moral development. Discuss the three levels of moral development given by Lawrence Kohlberg.
questions.answer: Moral development is the growth of a sense of right and wrong, including moral behaviour, reasoning and judgment. Kohlberg's levels: (1) Pre-moral level — children learn right and wrong from people around them; conduct is controlled by external factors such as approval and disapproval of authority, rewards and punishment, so behaviour is oriented to obedience and avoiding punishment. (2) Conventional morality — from middle childhood the capacity to understand relationships and moral codes grows; children follow society's rules but believe rules can be changed if they do not serve the common good. (3) Post-conventional morality — right and wrong are decided by one's own conscience; nothing is imposed from outside, and universal values such as the value of life are held highest, even above a law.

questions.q: How are language development, communication and emergent literacy interrelated? Discuss the pre-speech and speech forms of communication in children.
questions.answer: Language is the tool of communication and of thinking; listening and speaking (oral language) are the base for emergent literacy — reading and writing — and all grow together in a language-rich environment, so stimulation in the critical early years helps all of them. Pre-speech forms: crying (the first communication), cooing and babbling (from 6–7 months, repeated syllables like 'mama'), and gestures (pointing, waving, shaking the head). Speech forms: comprehension (children understand before they speak), pronunciation (clearer with age), vocabulary (grows tremendously in the early years) and sentence formation (two- or three-word phrases, then sentences, then complex sentences).

questions.q: Briefly explain the stages of cognitive development given by Piaget.
questions.answer: Sensorimotor (birth–2): infants learn through senses and reflexes like sucking and grasping, act intentionally, show deferred imitation and develop object permanence. Pre-operational (2–7): symbolic but pre-logical thought with animism, egocentrism and no reversibility or conservation. Concrete operational (7–11): logical thinking about concrete situations, decentering, reversibility, conservation and seriation; they understand others' viewpoints but find hypothetical problems hard. Formal operational (11+): abstract, flexible thought and hypothetico-deductive reasoning — forming hypotheses, finding all possible solutions and applying the best. The stages come in a fixed order and none is skipped, though the pace varies.
